posts.content:
Watching Spain lift the World Cup last week, one thought stayed with me. 

Plenty will be written about the players, the tactics, and the moments that decided it. But what stayed with me was something less visible. 

The best teams reduce the number of things they leave to chance. 

Players don't have to rediscover how to respond every time the game changes. Preparation, judgment, and coordination are built into how the team operates. 

That is an important distinction for business. 

For decades, companies have tried to improve performance by hiring exceptional people and giving them better software. Yet the quality of execution still varies enormously from one person, one deal, and one day to the next. 

The real opportunity isn't simply to add AI. 

It's to embed the preparation, context, and next-best actions of your strongest performers directly into the flow of work - so that great execution becomes more consistent across the entire team. 

That's what we're building at Outreach. 

Not software that simply watches the game. 

AI agents that help revenue teams play it better.

Unleash 2026 was different.

We deliberately made it smaller, more intimate, and more focused on one thing: helping customers learn from each other.

There is no shortage of AI hype right now. What is far more valuable is hearing directly from practitioners who are deploying agentic AI at scale, sharing what works, what doesn’t, the pitfalls to avoid, and the business outcomes they are achieving.

Over 3 days, customers, partners, analysts, and industry leaders came together to exchange ideas and experiences in an open and relaxed setting. The conversations were candid, practical, and deeply insightful.

We heard how organizations are using the Outreach agentic AI platform to generate pipeline, advance deals, improve forecast accuracy, retain customers, and coach teams more effectively.

One of my favorite moments came from David J Boyle at Cohesity. He shared the story of Alex Tan, a rep who was consistently crushing quota and helping teammates across the organization. The twist? Alex Tan wasn’t even a person. Alex Tan was an Outreach AI Agent!

Dennis Woodside, CEO of Freshworks, reminded us that every leader needs to get hands-on with AI. The best way to understand its potential is to use it yourself.

Chris Finlayson from OpenAI shared another important lesson: as companies embrace AI, the goal should be to augment and accelerate workflows, not rush to rebuild every application from scratch.

Thank you to all the speakers who generously shared their experiences, including Gianpaolo Fava and Rebecca Guise (ServiceNow), Utkarsh Bahadur (SAP), Lisa Eisenberg (Salesforce), Amita Gudipati (Renaissance Learning), Hamish Hill (SolarWinds), Katherine Stoverink Adams (Spectrum Business), Josh Harmon (Pushpay), James Terry (Indeed Flex), Thorsten Reichenberger (Siemens), Mariah Finleon and Matt Perry (SailPoint), Cody Harris and Ashita Saluja(Databricks), Katerina Ebert White (Hearst Newspapers) and everyone else who made this event so special.

And thank you to Nadia Rashid, Nithya Lakshmanan, Cathlyn Lang, Holly Simmons, and the entire Outreach team for bringing these conversations to life.

The future of agentic AI will be shaped by practitioners learning from one another, sharing what works, what doesn’t, and helping each other move from experimentation to real business impact. That was the spirit of Unleash, and it is what made this year’s event so special.

posts.content:
A few reflections from the past week in Europe.

The trip started in London, where I spent time with customers discussing the opportunities and challenges they see ahead. From there, I joined fellow CEOs in Paris at Bill McDermott's CEO Summit. As is often the case, some of the best conversations happened outside the formal sessions.

One thing stood out throughout the week.

Relationships still matter.

Whether meeting with customers in London or listening to perspectives from leaders in business, government, media, technology, and the arts in Paris, I was reminded that the best ideas often come from outside our own industries and areas of expertise.

One session that particularly stayed with me was a conversation with Refik Anadol. Much of my day-to-day thinking about AI is centered on business applications, helping people be more productive, make better decisions, and achieve better outcomes. Refik offered a very different perspective. He spoke about using custom AI models trained on carefully curated data to create new forms of artistic expression and experiences that can move people emotionally.

It was a reminder that AI is not just about efficiency and automation. It can also be a tool for creativity, inspiration, and perhaps even healing. That conversation opened my mind to possibilities well beyond the business use cases that most of us focus on every day.

Having my wife join me for part of the journey was also a reminder that business is ultimately about people. Whether with customers, colleagues, partners, or friends, the strongest relationships are built through personal connections and trust over time.

Technology will continue to change how we work.

Trust, relationships, creativity, and human connection remain timeless.

Onward to Monaco.

posts.content:
The enterprise software industry is undergoing a massive architectural shift. 
 
For decades, revenue leaders relied on stagnant point solutions to store data, track activities, and measure performance. Now, the market is moving rapidly toward platforms that take action. 
 
I recently sat down with Seth Marrs, Chief Strategy Officer at Sandler and the former Forrester analyst who helped create the revenue orchestration category, to unpack what this shift really means. A few themes stood out: 

- CRM remains the system of record. Revenue orchestration is where the work actually happens: conversations, emails, meetings, and AI-driven actions. 
- Reps spend only 26-30% of their time selling. AI agents are the most direct solution to that capacity problem. 
- The CRO of the future is a revenue orchestrator, running an intelligent system where humans and agents work together toward shared outcomes. 
 
As Seth put it: "The source of truth to me for everything that's happening in a deal, conversations, emails, phone calls, that is Outreach." 
 
That's exactly why we're building Outreach as the agentic AI platform for revenue teams. Agents amplify seller, handling the administrative burden so humans can focus on strategy, negotiation, and relationships. 
 
The next chapter of sales will not be built by adding more tools.

⭐ The Rise of the AI GTM Architect ⭐ 

This week, during our senior leadership discussions, we had an insightful conversation with Seth Marrs about how revenue orchestration is becoming a core pillar of designing revenue growth, especially as organizations leverage AI at scale.

This shift is redefining Revenue Operations. RevOps is no longer just an enabler of execution—it is increasingly responsible for owning the successful implementation of AI‑led GTM strategies. As a result, new responsibilities and functions are emerging within RevOps. 

At Outreach, we’ve started to identify one of these roles as the GTM Architect. As we began implementing AI agents within our GTM motion, it became clear that organizations need a dedicated role to design, structure, and govern how AI agents operate across the revenue engine. 

We call this role the GTM Architect because it requires designing AI behavior that complements sellers, reinforces their strengths, and mimics the most effective and authentic aspects of how great sellers engage buyers.
AI agents are successful only when they extend a seller’s reach in a natural, trustworthy way—not when they replace them.
To do this well, the GTM Architect must combine several disciplines:
✅  First, data and audience understanding: defining the ICP, personas, challenges, and problems we’re trying to solve.
✅  Second, agent behavior design: shaping how the AI behaves, how it communicates, and how prompts and flows are structured to feel human and relevant.
✅  Third, the GTM motion itself: partnering with Marketing and Sales leadership to design campaigns and approaches that are compelling for the market.
✅  Finally, infrastructure and signals: ensuring the AI can access the right data and signals across the organization to make intelligent decisions.

In many ways, this role mirrors how data scientists emerged years ago—combining multiple disciplines to unlock value. The GTM Architect unlocks business value within the sales organization.

Importantly, this is not an engineering role. The goal isn’t heavy custom coding, but leveraging purpose‑built platforms to design and orchestrate GTM motions. Think of it as the difference between building an instrument and playing one. The GTM Architect is the conductor.

Liz Campbell Libby Fleming Kamille Ramirez Matt Cimmino Nala Comstock Murugan Namasivayam Toni Eddleman Sarah Foster Victoria Early
